turns.doctor_question: Hello, and welcome. I'm Dr. [Name], a psychiatrist. What brings you in to see me today?
turns.patient_response:
Well, hello Doctor. I suppose I came in because... well, it's been getting really difficult at the store lately. I'm a retail supervisor, have been for quite a while, and a big part of my day-to-day is getting the team together to explain the inventory numbers or sort out the weekend schedule. It should be simple, right? I've got a bachelor's degree, I know how to run a sales floor. But recently, when I stand up there to just explain the basic stock numbers or who is working Saturday, my words just... they start jumping around on me. 

I'll start off talking about the delivery trucks, which is normal, but then somehow I'm on to Thursdays, and from Thursdays I'm suddenly talking out loud about the church grill, and then I'm going on about my boss’s tone of voice when he called me earlier... and I'll stop and realize that the whole staff, they're just staring at me. People look at me like they absolutely can’t follow what I’m saying. And I try to pull it back, I really do, but it’s like my mouth is just connecting all these things that make sense to me in that split second, but to them, it's just a tangled mess. It's embarrassing, frankly, to be standing there in front of the retail workers and have them looking at me like I'm speaking a completely different language, so I knew I needed to come in and talk to somebody about it.

symptom_reasoning.S021: The patient describes their speech jumping rapidly between unrelated topics (trucks, Thursdays, church grill, boss's tone) making it impossible for others to follow, which is a clear presentation of disorganized thinking and loose associations.

turns.doctor_question: When your thoughts are jumping around like that during these moments at work, do they feel like they're moving really fast—like your mind is racing ahead of what you're saying?
turns.patient_response:
Racing... no, I wouldn't say racing. It's not like my mind is on fast-forward or anything like that. I mean, I remember back when I was getting my bachelor's, pulling all-nighters for exams, drinking whole pots of coffee, and my brain going a mile a minute—that was racing. But this... this is entirely different. 

It’s actually quite the opposite in terms of speed. I feel like I'm talking at a perfectly normal, measured pace, just exactly like I am with you right now. I'll be standing there in the breakroom—we have this little huddle area right by the time clocks, we usually do our meetings around 8:45 AM right before the main doors open to the public—and I'm just calmly going down my clipboard. It's not the speed, Doctor, it's the... the tracks. 

It's like I'm driving a train at a perfectly safe, steady speed, but the tracks just keep switching without me pulling the lever. So I'll be talking about the delivery pallets in the back room, and my brain just naturally, smoothly transitions to the wooden pallets we used for the church barbecue last summer, and then to the mustard we had there, and then to the yellow promotional shirts the cashiers are supposed to wear on weekends. It all feels completely logical and paced normally to me in the moment. There's no rush, no pressure pushing my words out or making me trip over my tongue because I'm thinking too fast. It's just that the destination completely changes while I'm mid-sentence, and I don't even realize I've gone off the map until I see my assistant manager, Greg, giving me this thoroughly confused look from the back row. 

So, no, they aren't racing ahead of me at all. I don't have that feeling of my mind outrunning my mouth. They're just... taking these elaborate detours, I suppose you could say, but at a very leisurely, normal speed.

symptom_reasoning.S021: The patient describes derailment and loose associations, where their speech smoothly but illogically transitions from one unrelated topic to another (e.g., delivery pallets to mustard to yellow shirts) mid-sentence.

symptom_reasoning.S038: The patient explicitly denies having racing thoughts, stating their mind is not on fast-forward and their thoughts are not outrunning their mouth.

turns.patient_response:

I mean, the pallets are wood, the barbecue used wood, mustard is yellow, the shirts are yellow... it just flows from one to the next. 

But then, when I stop and look at Greg—he's my assistant manager, I think I mentioned him, good guy, been with the company for about six years now, started as a cashier and worked his way up—when I look at Greg and see his face just completely scrunched up in confusion, that's when I realize it. That's when I stop and think, "Wait, why on earth am I talking about mustard when we're supposed to be going over the holiday weekend schedule?" 

So, no, I don't think there's some grand, meaningful reason they're connected. Not in hindsight. I mean, I'm not standing there thinking the universe is sending me a message through the mustard or anything like that. I know it's just my brain making these... leaps. But it's so frustrating because it doesn't feel like a leap when it's happening. It feels like I'm walking a straight path, but then I turn around and see I've wandered off into the woods, and everyone else is still standing on the trail wondering where I went. 

It's just so embarrassing, honestly. Especially because I've always prided myself on being a clear communicator. You have to be in retail, you know? You have to be able to give clear directions, especially when things get busy. Like during the back-to-school rush, or the holidays... if you aren't clear, the whole floor falls apart. And now here I am, rambling about church barbecues. It's just... I don't know why my brain is making these associations, but I do know they don't actually mean anything. turns.doctor_question: Have you ever heard voices speaking to you when no one else was around, or seen things that other people couldn't see?
turns.patient_response:

My hearing is perfectly fine—well, maybe a little ringing in the left ear sometimes, but I went to an audiologist about that two years ago and he said it was just mild tinnitus, probably from when I used to go to all those rock concerts in my twenties. I saw The Who back in '82, you know, and we were right up by the speakers. My ears rang for three days straight after that one. But as far as hearing voices speaking to me when I'm alone in the house, or in the stockroom? No, absolutely not. 

And I don't see things that aren't there, either. My vision is actually quite good for my age, I just use readers when I'm looking at the tiny print on the inventory sheets. You wouldn't believe how small they print the SKUs on the new shipping labels. It's ridiculous, really, they try to cram so much information onto a two-by-four-inch sticker that you practically need a magnifying glass. But no, I'm not hallucinating people or shadows or anything of that sort. 

It's really just the talking, Doctor. Just the way my words get all tangled up when I'm trying to explain things to the team. That's the only thing that's out of the ordinary. Everything else—my senses, my hearing, my vision—it's all completely normal. I live alone, well, just me and my golden retriever, Buster. He's eight now, getting a little gray around the muzzle, but he's a good boy. And if I were hearing voices or seeing things in the house, I think Buster would let me know, right? We were moving all the endcaps—those big corrugated cardboard displays that take absolutely forever to assemble because the tabs never line up right with the slots, you know the ones I mean? Greg actually pulled me aside later that day in the breakroom to ask if I was feeling alright. So it didn't just happen overnight like a light switch flipping, it sort of crept up on me, but it's been a solid six months of it being a real issue at work. Retail takes a lot out of you, especially at my age, and when you're on your feet on that hard commercial linoleum for eight, sometimes ten hours a day, it drains you. I even went out and bought new heavy-duty inserts for my work shoes thinking maybe the physical fatigue was just getting to my head and making me lose my train of thought. He expected us to predict foot traffic based on these corporate algorithms that just don't apply to our specific location, and if you were off by even a fraction of a percent on your payroll budget, you'd get this long, passive-aggressive email copying everyone in the region. 

So I was spending hours, I mean hours, in the back office staring at these spreadsheets, trying to make our schedule match his impossible targets without short-staffing the floor. And that... that really took a toll. That’s when I started not feeling quite like myself. Like you said, I was definitely more withdrawn. Usually, I'm a very hands-on supervisor, I like being out on the floor, joking with the cashiers, helping customers find things. But I started just shutting my office door and hiding in there. 

And my sleep went completely out the window. I'd be lying in bed at two in the morning, wide awake, just calculating overtime pay in my head and worrying about the next quarter's forecast. I even stopped taking Buster to the dog park on weekends because I was just so completely drained and preoccupied. I just didn't have the energy for it, which isn't like me at all. So, yes, the talking part, the getting my words tangled up on the floor, that's been six months. But that underlying feeling of just being overloaded, of pulling away from everyone and not feeling right in my own head? That’s been brewing for about 11 months, ever since those new scheduling demands started coming down from corporate.

turns.doctor_question: Before these 11 months started—going back further into your past, maybe years ago—has there ever been a time when you experienced anything like what we've been talking about? Before these 11 months? No, no, nothing like this at all. I mean, if you look back at my career, I have been in retail management for over thirty years now. Right out of college with my bachelor degree, I went straight into a management trainee program for one of the big department stores. Back then, and really up until this last year, my mind was an absolute steel trap. You could ask me the SKU number for a specific blender we sold three seasons ago, and I would just rattle it off for you. I never had these moments where my words would scatter, or where I would freeze up in the aisles. I was the guy they sent to fix underperforming stores because I could walk in, assess the floor plan, reorganize the stockroom, and communicate exactly what needed to be done to a staff of fifty people without missing a single beat. 

And as far as believing things that were not true, or having unusual perceptions... no, absolutely nothing like that. I have always been a very grounded, practical guy. You have to be in this line of work. It is all numbers, profit margins, foot traffic, shrink percentages. There is no room for getting carried away with strange ideas when you are trying to reconcile the registers at midnight on a Tuesday. 

I remember back in two thousand and eight, during the recession, we had this massive corporate restructuring, and they merged three districts into one. It was chaos. Absolute chaos. People were losing their jobs, the inventory systems were completely incompatible, and I was working sixty, seventy hours a week just trying to keep my location afloat. You would think if my brain was ever going to crack, or if I was going to start having disorganized thoughts or weird beliefs, it would have been then. The stress was unbelievable. But even then, I was sharp. I kept my head down, I communicated perfectly clearly, and I ran the floor like clockwork. 

So no, before this recent stretch, this whole eleven month nightmare we have been talking about, I have never dealt with anything even remotely like this. Not in my twenties, not in my thirties, never. My mind was always my strongest asset. Always.
